subject: Business Models
title: SaaS: Software as a Service
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: SaaS: Software as a Service.

hook.text: Microsoft Office once cost $499 per box. Now it's $10/month forever. You never stop paying.

buildup.text: SaaS replaced one-time software purchases with monthly subscriptions. Revenue became predictable.

discovery.text: The key metric is Annual Recurring Revenue. Investors value SaaS at 10-20x ARR, far above one-time sales.

twist.text: You pay $120/year for software that used to cost $499 once. After 4 years, you've paid more.

climax.text: SaaS companies dominate tech valuations because predictable revenue is worth more than spiky sales.

punchline.text: Buy once for $499, or rent forever at $120/year. Renting won.

quiz.question: Why do investors value SaaS companies so highly?

details.summary: Software as a Service delivers applications over the internet on a subscription basis, replacing one-time license sales with recurring monthly or annual revenue. SaaS transformed software economics by shifting from upfront capital expenses to predictable operational expenses.
details.whyItMatters: SaaS is the dominant software business model generating over 300 billion in annual revenue globally. Its recurring revenue, high margins, and scalability make it the foundation of modern enterprise technology investment.
takeaways: Subscriptions create predictable recurring revenue streams for vendors
Cloud delivery eliminates installation and maintenance for customers
SaaS businesses are valued on annual recurring revenue growth rates

faq.question: What makes SaaS businesses so highly valued by investors?
faq.answer: Recurring revenue is predictable and compounds over time. Gross margins typically exceed 70%. Customer switching costs are high once workflows depend on the tool. Revenue growth with net retention above 100% means existing customers spend more each year automatically.

faq.question: What are the key metrics for measuring SaaS business health?
faq.answer: Annual recurring revenue measures total subscription base. Net revenue retention shows expansion within existing customers. Customer acquisition cost versus lifetime value measures unit economics. Churn rate tracks customer losses. Rule of 40 combines growth rate plus profit margin.
